client: I've been really struggling since my dog passed away last month. He was with me for eleven years, and now everything just feels... flat, I guess. I'm going through the motions at work and at home, but nothing feels enjoyable anymore, and I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change that.
therapist: Losing a companion of eleven years is a profound loss, and what you're describing — that flatness, going through the motions, nothing feeling enjoyable — sounds a lot like grief doing exactly what grief does. It makes a lot of sense that you'd feel uncertain whether talking will help, especially when everything feels so muted right now. I'm wondering, when you think about him, is there a particular moment or memory that comes up most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I keep coming back to this one evening where we were just sitting on the couch together, him curled up against my leg, and I wasn't even doing anything special — just watching some dumb show. It felt so ordinary then, and now it feels like the most important moment in the world, which is kind of cruel in a way. I guess I didn't know how much I needed that kind of quiet company until it was gone.
therapist: That memory is so tender — there's something really meaningful about how that quiet, "ordinary" moment has become a kind of treasure now, even if it hurts to hold it. What you're describing, that realization of needing that gentle, steady presence, feels like a really important thing to know about yourself. I'm curious — is there anything in your life right now that offers even a small echo of that kind of quiet comfort?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to just say "no, nothing" and move on. There's my cat, I guess — she sometimes just comes and sits near me when I'm having a bad night, and there's something about that that feels a little like what you're describing. But it also makes me sad, because it's a cat, and I don't know if that's kind of pathetic, that the closest thing I have to that steady presence is an animal.
therapist: There's nothing pathetic about that at all — connection and comfort are real regardless of where they come from, and your cat showing up for you on hard nights is genuinely meaningful. I'd actually gently push back on that "just a cat" thought, because it sounds like a part of you is dismissing something that's actually helping you, maybe because you feel like you shouldn't need it. What do you think that voice is about — the one that wants to minimize what she gives you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I guess that voice is probably about feeling like I should be able to handle things on my own, like needing comfort from a cat is proof that I'm failing at being a normal functioning adult with actual human relationships. It's embarrassing to admit that a small animal is sometimes the only reason I don't feel completely alone at night. But maybe you're right that I'm dismissing it, because when she curls up next to me I do actually feel something real, not just like I'm pretending it helps.
therapist: What you just said at the end feels really important — that it's *real*, not pretend — and I want to stay with that for a moment, because that's not a small thing to recognize. The idea that needing comfort makes you a "failing adult" sounds like a really harsh standard you're holding yourself to, one that most people would never apply to a friend in grief. I'm curious where that belief comes from — that being self-sufficient is the measure of whether you're doing okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know exactly where it comes from, but I think it's been there for a long time — like, asking for help always felt like admitting you couldn't handle things, and that was something to be ashamed of. My dad was pretty stoic, never really talked about feelings, and I guess I picked up the message that strong people just push through. But hearing you say it out loud like that, comparing it to how I'd treat a friend... I mean, I wouldn't tell a friend they're failing because they're grieving and lonely. That does feel kind of unfair when I put it that way.
therapist: It sounds like something genuinely shifted just now — recognizing that the rule you've been living by, that needing help means weakness, was something you absorbed rather than something you chose. That's actually a really significant moment. I'm wondering, if you could start to loosen that old message just a little, what might it look like to treat yourself with even a fraction of the kindness you'd offer a grieving friend?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, part of me does feel something shift when you put it that way. But when I try to imagine actually being kind to myself about needing help, it just feels... hollow, like I'd be going through the motions without really believing it. I guess I'm not sure how you treat yourself kindly when some part of you still thinks the old message is true.
therapist: That feeling of "going through the motions" with self-compassion is actually really common — it doesn't mean it's not working, it just means the old belief is still loud enough to drown out the new one, and that takes time to change. You don't have to *believe* it fully yet to start practicing it, in the same way you don't have to feel motivated to go through a routine before the feeling eventually follows the action. I'm wondering if there's one very small, specific moment this week where you could experiment with that — not forcing the feeling, but just trying on a gentler response to yourself and seeing what happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess it makes sense logically that the feeling doesn't have to come first. But honestly, the moment I try to be gentler with myself, there's this voice that immediately jumps in and says I'm just making excuses for being a bad friend. Like, I missed my friend's birthday last month because I was too anxious to leave the house, and every time I try to let myself off the hook even a little, it feels like I'm just... justifying being a terrible person.
therapist: That voice that calls you a "terrible person" for missing a birthday while you were grieving and anxious — that's not an honest assessment of who you are, that's the old message turning up the volume right when you're most vulnerable. Missing something because you were struggling isn't evidence of being a bad friend; it's evidence that you were having a hard time, which is exactly what we've been talking about. I'm curious — if your friend knew what last month was really like for you, do you think they would use the words "terrible person"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... no, probably not. She's actually pretty understanding, and if she knew how bad things were last month, she'd probably feel bad that I hadn't told her. But that's almost the problem, right? Because now I feel guilty for not reaching out to her when I was struggling, like I kept her out and then also let her down, and it just feels like I can't win either way.
therapist: That "can't win" feeling is really worth pausing on, because it's a sign that the rules you're playing by might be set up in a way that makes it impossible to ever be okay — kept her out *and* let her down can't both be equally your fault. What's interesting is that you've actually just identified something important: she's understanding, she'd want to know, which means the door isn't closed. I'm wondering what feels like the bigger obstacle to reaching out to her now — the fear of explaining why you went quiet, or something else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think the bigger obstacle is... honestly, I don't even know how to start that conversation. Like, what do I say — "hey, sorry I disappeared for three months, I was drowning and too ashamed to tell you"? That feels so awkward and exposing, and I'm scared that even if she's understanding in the moment, she'll quietly think less of me afterward.
therapist: The fear that someone will say the right thing but secretly think less of you — that's such a painful place to be, because it means even a good response wouldn't fully feel safe. It's worth noticing that this fear might be the same voice again, the one that's already decided you're failing, and now it's putting that judgment into her mouth before she's even had a chance to respond. What do you actually know about her, from your history together, that might be evidence about how she'd really hold this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, she's never actually made me feel stupid for struggling with things before. There was that time I told her I was overwhelmed at work and she just... listened, didn't try to fix it or make it weird. But I keep thinking, this is different, this is lonelier somehow, and maybe she has a limit to how much of my mess she can take before she starts pulling back.
therapist: You actually have real evidence about her — she's shown you who she is when you're struggling, and it wasn't judgment, it was presence. But I notice there's something that sounds almost braced in how you're talking about this, like you're waiting for the moment she finally confirms your worst fear, even though she hasn't given you a reason to expect that. I'm wondering if that fear of "reaching her limit" is less about her and more about a deeper worry that your pain is too much — that *you* are too much — for someone to stay with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
